source.title: Spectral Bias in Practice: The Role of Function Frequency in Generalization
source.authors: Sara Fridovich-Keil; Raphael Gontijo Lopes; R. Roelofs

record.file_problem: none; full paper text and appendix are present
record.tranche_reason: Measures learned function frequency and its association with test accuracy across training and data conditions, a different measurement from the listed versions’ generalization-gap measures.
record.gate_note: The paper measures spectral properties of learned classifiers and reports test accuracies, but does not measure training-versus-test error gaps or test the random-label memorization/generalization claim. Its frequency-versus-accuracy associations are relevant to generalization but do not directly instantiate V1–V8. The paper reports no numerical frequency values in the text; figure-only measurements are not extracted as rows. Explicit textual figure summaries support the rows below.
record.test_reason: The study measures spectral bias and associations between function frequency and held-out accuracy, rather than any outcome specified by V1–V8. Its width comparisons do not establish zero training error or widening beyond the interpolation threshold. Structured label-smoothing noise is not fixed random-label memorization, and input-space function smoothness is not magnitude-aware weight sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' conclusions about frequency separation, accuracy, and class diversity. It omits their additional central finding that modern CNNs exhibit spectral bias, with lower-frequency label-smoothing functions learned more readily. These are frequency-proxy results and associations, not tests of V1–V8 or evidence that frequency separation causes better generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The paper measures frequency proxies along interpolated inputs and with label-smoothing noise, rather than training-test error gaps, random-label memorization, or the interventions in V1–V8.
record.method_sensitivity: Frequency outcomes vary with architecture, training time, training-set size, augmentation strength and method, self-distillation, ImageNet class diversity, and model family; CoAtNets show no clear class-diversity correlation.

fits_no_version.finding: Frequency separation increases during training across the tested CIFAR-10 and ImageNet models. CIFAR-10 accuracy improvements accompany lower within-class and higher between-class frequencies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Function frequency separates within-class from between-class behavior as image classifiers train and improve.

fits_no_version.finding: More training data, more effective augmentation, and self-distillation increase frequency separation or reduce within-class frequency; excessive Mixup can reverse the smoothing trend.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training choices associated with better accuracy also change the spatial distribution of learned function frequency.

fits_no_version.finding: Most tested ImageNet models have higher within-class function frequencies in more diverse classes; the two CoAtNets show no clear correlation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within-class function frequency often tracks class diversity, with architecture-dependent exceptions.

fits_no_version.finding: Models learn lower-frequency structured label-smoothing noise more readily; greater width facilitates fitting higher-frequency noise, while stronger weight decay delays it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Modern image classifiers exhibit spectral bias whose strength depends on width and weight decay.

record.problems: The paper uses coarse proxy measures of frequency along selected pixel-space interpolation paths, aggregates across many paths and classes, and notes these paths can leave the natural-image manifold. The reported frequency outcomes are mostly presented in figures; numerical values are not stated in the text. It does not measure training-test error gaps.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-only frequency measurements without textual descriptions and specific figure values were not extracted because the text does not provide assignable numbers. Label-smoothing noise-fitting plots (Figures 3, 5, 8, 9, 12) measure learnability of imposed label noise, not the versions’ named outcomes. Figure summaries with textual result descriptions are included where they directly report measured frequency outcomes.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fixed random-label fitting and chance held-out accuracy, compared with natural-label generalization under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond an established zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and interventions on local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers under specified tuning conditions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects, including small datasets, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbation tolerance, its association with training-test gaps, and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The absence of training-test gap measurements alone does not exclude every version: several versions concern held-out performance directly. Exclusion here rests on the missing claim-specific comparisons and interventions. Original-source citations provide context but no independent test.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out performance under the same training recipes.
Test error as width increases past the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected test-error comparison and local-connectivity interventions.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer held-out performance.
Large- versus small-batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of training-test gaps.
Removal of memorized training examples and resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: CIFAR-10 models (all six tested models; aggregate textual result)
rows.size_stated: six convolutional neural networks; specific model sizes not stated here
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; training duration varies
rows.operation_detail: Compared function frequency along within-class and between-class interpolation paths as training proceeds.
rows.measure: Frequency separation between within-class and between-class paths
rows.value: All six models become higher-frequency between-class and lower-frequency within-class throughout training; frequency separation increases as accuracy improves.
rows.note: Frequency separation and accuracy association are stated; this is not a measurement of training-test error gap.
rows.check: The textual result is accurate, but frequency separation does not measure any listed version.

rows.subject: wrn_160
rows.operation_detail: Compared interpolation frequencies while varying the number of training examples.
rows.value: Increasing the number of training examples decreases function frequency within-class and slightly increases it between-class.
rows.note: The result concerns frequency, not the training-test error gap.
rows.check: Figure 13 and Section A.3.5 report this result for all six CIFAR-10 models, not only wrn_160; wrn_160 is the main-text example in Figure 6. The frequency outcome fits no listed version.

rows.subject: CIFAR-10 models (all six tested models; aggregate textual result)
rows.size_stated: six convolutional neural networks; specific model sizes not stated here
rows.stage_stated: trained on CIFAR-10 with data augmentation conditions
rows.operation_detail: Compared interpolation frequencies across data augmentation strengths and methods.
rows.measure: Function frequency and its separation between path types
rows.baseline: less effective or no augmentation, as ordered in the figure
rows.value: More effective augmentation produces lower within-class frequency; test accuracy and frequency separation increase across the reported ordering.
rows.check: Accurate frequency and accuracy summary, but augmentation alone does not test V6's dropout or joint dropout-and-weight-decay removal comparison.

rows.subject: CIFAR-10 models (all six tested models; aggregate textual result)
rows.size_stated: six convolutional neural networks; specific model sizes not stated here
rows.operation_detail: Compared within-class interpolation frequencies across Mixup strengths.
rows.value: Modest Mixup produces a lower-frequency within-class function, while Mixup that is too strong can induce higher within-class frequencies.
rows.note: The paper gives no numerical frequency values in the text; no train-test gap is measured.
rows.check: The result concerns Mixup strength, not dropout strength or another listed intervention.

rows.subject: CIFAR-10 models (all six tested models; aggregate textual result)
rows.size_stated: six convolutional neural networks; specific model sizes not stated here
rows.operation_detail: Compared student and teacher interpolation frequencies and test accuracy.
rows.measure: Within-class and between-class function frequency; test accuracy
rows.value: The student is lower-frequency within-class, has slightly higher frequency between-class, and has higher test accuracy than its teacher.
rows.note: Accuracy is compared, but training error and the train-test gap are not reported in this result.
rows.check: Self-distillation changes function frequency and held-out accuracy, but tests no listed version.

rows.subject: ImageNet models (all ten tested models; aggregate textual result)
rows.size_stated: ten pretrained models; architecture-specific sizes listed in Appendix A.1
rows.stage_stated: pretrained ImageNet checkpoints; training checkpoints examined over time
rows.operation_detail: Compared frequency separation along within-class and between-class interpolation paths over training.
rows.value: All ten models increase frequency separation between within-class and between-class paths during training.
rows.note: The result measures frequency separation, not a generalization gap.
rows.check: Accurate separation summary. Within-class frequency does not decrease for every ImageNet model; CoAtNets can increase on both path types. Neither trend measures a listed version.

rows.subject: ImageNet models (all ten tested models; aggregate textual result)
rows.size_stated: ten pretrained models; architecture-specific sizes listed in Appendix A.1
rows.operation_detail: Related within-class interpolation frequency to class diversity measured by C-Scores.
rows.measure: Association between class diversity and function frequency
rows.value: Most models have higher function frequencies within more diverse classes; the two CoAtNet models show no clear correlation.
rows.note: The reported model-level exception is explicit; this is not a measurement of train-test error gap.
rows.check: The reported correlation and CoAtNet exceptions are accurate, but 'partial' describes an unlisted frequency-diversity claim. C-Scores are not the memorization-based removal intervention in V8.
